item.title: Why Can't We Stop Scrolling?
item.description:
Social Media

Why Can't We Stop Scrolling?

Our society's infatuation with short-form media is stronger than ever.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Social media addiction is not yet recognized by the DSM-5-TR as a true behavioral addiction.
  • The endless feed that social media platforms create causes a psychological response similar to gambling.
  • Dopamine's role in social media use is unclear but many studies are examining the relationship.
  • Social media rewards our excessive use in multiple ways.

Regrettably, it’s everywhere–at the stoplight, on the train, across the dinner table, on your own couch. It’s a phenomenon that transcends cultures, geographical divides, and generations. Doomscrolling.

Doomscrolling–a colloquial term for mindlessly swiping through your social media feed–has become a ritualistic part of many individuals’ daily lives. Specifically, short-form media such as TikToks, Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts, and others have taken over the screens of our smartphones and, consequently, much of our lives.

Why do we doomscroll and what keeps us coming back? Researchers are trying to figure that out, but the answer may be more complex than we realize.

1. The Social Media Slot Machine

Although the DSM-5-TR does not officially recognize social media addiction as a true behavioral addiction, many researchers have been attempting to address the infatuation that we have with our phones regardless of the lack of an officially recognized diagnosis. Currently, the only recognized behavioral addiction is gambling, yet the two share much in common. In fact, much of the current research on social media obsession springs from prior research on gambling.

Source: AI-Generated

One of the addictive features of gambling is the intermittent nature of the reward: winning only occasionally is exactly what keeps people coming back to the slot machine. Similarly, studies have examined how the variability of our feeds contributes to our urge to engage with the so-called “infinite scroll,” a phenomenon termed the partial reinforcement system. Not every video is going to provide you with content you want to see, which not only makes a good or funny video that much better, but also creates sustained reward expectancy, which refers to the anticipation you may feel as you scroll to the next video to see what awaits you. The variability is precisely what keeps us going, just as the tantalizing uncertainty satiates a slot machine player.

2. Dopamine’s Role in the Rush

Dopamine, one of the neurotransmitters that plays a major role in our biological response to reward, has been intensely studied for its role in addiction. When it comes to social media and our consumption of never-ending short-form videos, the role of dopamine is not well understood.

One study surprisingly found that dopamine synthesis was indirectly correlated with high social media screen time; that is, the more time individuals spent on social media platforms, the less dopamine was produced during PET scans measuring putamen activity. While not suggesting any level of causation, this correlation goes against the common assumption that impulsive activities produce a burst of dopamine that explains addiction.

article continues after advertisement

Another study, however, found that increased social media usage showed no correlation with higher signal intensity seen on neuromelanin-sensitive MRI, a marker that serves as a proxy for measuring dopamine synthesis. Both of these studies show that social media use, though extremely similar to other forms of behavioral addiction, may have a more complex relationship with dopaminergic pathways than we initially suspected.

Source: Mohamed Hassan/Pixabay

3. Reward Comes in Many Forms

When we are scrolling social media, the return is not as straightforward as a dollar amount on a casino voucher. The satisfaction of the scroll is multifaceted: the reward comes in the form of novelty, comedy, information, social knowledge, anticipation, boredom cessation—you name it. It is no wonder that studies struggle to quantify our newest societal addiction, considering it serves so many unquantifiable purposes in our subconscious. However, perhaps identifying what it is we find individually enjoyable about our social media interactions is the key to breaking up with our doomscroll.

item.title: Conflict (Done Right) Can Enhance Closeness
item.description:
Relationships

Conflict (Done Right) Can Enhance Closeness

How navigating disagreement can help build trust in your relationships.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Avoiding conflict can feel safe, but it may prevent relationships from becoming closer.
  • Disagreement gives us information about how others respond when we're vulnerable.
  • Navigating conflict successfully can help build trust over time.

Most of us don't think of conflict as a relationship-building activity. We tend to view a disagreement as evidence that something has gone wrong. If the relationship is strong, we should always get along, right?

Avoiding conflict can seem like the safest way to protect a relationship. This can look like letting the irritating comment go or going along with the group when making plans. In the short term, you keep the peace, but you may also have missed an opportunity to become closer.

Conflict, when handled well, allows two people to learn something important about their relationship. Through conflict, you collect evidence that you can disagree, disappoint each other, and even get angry with each other without threatening the relationship itself.

Why Conflict Feels So Risky

The first time you have a disagreement with someone, it’s scary—you don’t know what’s going to happen. When you tell someone you're hurt, ask them to change their behavior, or disagree with something they've said, you don’t know how they’ll respond. They could become angry. They could tell you that you're being unreasonable. They could storm out.

For people who are particularly sensitive to rejection, perhaps due to past experiences, uncertainty in relationships can feel intolerable. Staying quiet provides immediate relief because you’re not putting yourself in a position to be on the receiving end of a negative response. You may even tell yourself that you're being easygoing or protecting the relationship.

Unfortunately, avoiding outward conflict doesn't make the underlying problem disappear. Small frustrations can turn into resentment, and other people may have no idea that anything is wrong. Perhaps more importantly, you never get to learn whether the relationship actually could have survived the disagreement you were so afraid to have.

Conflict Gives Us New Information

Imagine a friend repeatedly cancels plans at the last minute. You value the friendship, so you keep telling her it's fine even though you're increasingly frustrated. Tired of feeling disappointed, you start to decline invitations, and the two of you grow apart.

Now imagine that, instead, you tell her that her behavior upset you. Maybe you say something like, "I really want to spend time with you, but when you cancel plans at the last minute, it's hard to feel like I’m a priority for you."

Having a conversation like that may feel uncomfortable, or even terrifying. But it gives you the opportunity to see what actually happens when you share your genuine feelings in a relationship. Maybe your friend apologizes. Maybe she explains that she’s been dealing with a sick parent who calls on her at unpredictable times. Maybe she shuts down because she’s angry.

Whatever happens, you now have information you couldn't get by avoiding the conversation. Knowing how other people respond in the face of conflict is important data that you can use to decide how close you want to be with them.

Disagreement Can Build Trust

We often think trust needs to exist before we can be vulnerable in our relationships. In practice, trust is built through the experience of being vulnerable and discovering how the other person handles it.

Small conflicts provide opportunities to collect this evidence. When you tell someone that they’ve hurt you and they don't turn it back around on you, you learn it is OK to express your feelings. When you disagree and they remain curious about your perspective, you learn that it’s safe to express yourself.

Over time, those experiences can change what you expect from other people. Instead of needing constant agreement as proof that a relationship is secure, you begin to trust that differences can exist without threatening the connection.

Closeness Requires Some Friction

A conflict-free relationship isn't necessarily a close one. Sometimes it means that neither person is saying what they really think.

Meaningful relationships require us to discover that we can be two separate people and still remain connected. We can have different preferences, needs, and opinions, and still develop closeness.

Handled well, conflict gives us the opportunity to collect evidence. The disagreement itself isn't what creates closeness. It's what happens next that matters: You learn that you can be honest about your experience, hear a different perspective, and remain connected.

item.title: Can Health Problems Trigger Eating Disorders?
item.description:
Eating Disorders

Can Health Problems Trigger Eating Disorders?

How physical illness can increase food anxiety and trigger eating disorders.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Eating disorders can emerge in the context of gastrointestinal, autoimmune, and other health conditions.
  • Necessary dietary changes can sometimes expand into increasingly restrictive and fear-driven eating.
  • Treatment should address eating disorder symptoms while continuing to take medical concerns seriously.

Eating disorders are often associated with dieting, body dissatisfaction, or a desire to lose weight, but not every eating disorder begins that way.

For some people, difficulties with food begin in the context of a genuine physical health problem. Gastrointestinal disorders, autoimmune conditions, food allergies or intolerances, chronic pain, and other illnesses can significantly change a person's experience of eating. Food may become associated with pain, nausea, bloating, bowel changes, or other uncomfortable and unpredictable symptoms. Medical treatment may also require significant dietary changes.

Paying attention to symptoms and following appropriate dietary recommendations are not eating disorder behaviors. But for some people, this necessary vigilance begins to expand, with more foods eliminated, greater anxiety about eating, and increasing attention to physical sensations. Eventually, it can become difficult to determine where appropriate health management ends and an eating disorder begins.

Food and Fear

Repeatedly feeling unwell after eating can have a powerful effect on how someone approaches food. A person who experiences abdominal pain or nausea after meals may understandably begin trying to identify what caused it. One food is eliminated, then another. Eating at restaurants may begin to feel risky because ingredients and preparation are less predictable, and foods prepared by other people can become difficult to trust.

Restricting food may also provide a sense of control when physical symptoms otherwise feel unpredictable, particularly because eating less or avoiding certain foods may actually reduce some symptoms, at least temporarily. Avoidance can also reduce anxiety about what might happen after eating, which can further reinforce restriction.

Over time, the person may become increasingly convinced that the safest approach is to eat less and avoid more foods.

Expanding Restrictions

This process can be particularly difficult to recognize when dietary changes were originally recommended by a healthcare professional. Some medical conditions legitimately require avoiding particular foods, while others may involve temporary elimination diets or dietary trials intended to clarify the relationship between foods and symptoms.

Problems can arise when restrictions begin expanding beyond what the medical condition requires. Foods that were never medically restricted may start to feel unsafe, or the person may become reluctant to reintroduce foods even when their medical team recommends doing so. Minor or ambiguous physical sensations may prompt additional eliminations, while rules around ingredients, preparation, timing, or portion sizes become increasingly rigid.

article continues after advertisement

At some point, it may be difficult for the person to distinguish between foods that need to be avoided for medical reasons and foods they have become afraid to eat, especially when the distinction is not entirely clear.

Increased Body Vigilance

Chronic illness can also change the way someone pays attention to their body. When symptoms are unpredictable, it makes sense to notice what happens after eating, but sustained monitoring can gradually become consuming.

Someone may repeatedly check their stomach for bloating, evaluate fullness, monitor bowel function, track changes in energy, or closely analyze whether something feels different after a meal. Physical sensations that once would have attracted little attention can begin to feel highly significant. Fullness may become alarming, bloating may trigger anxiety, and a change in digestion may prompt extensive analysis about what was eaten and what needs to be avoided next.

As this pattern progresses, more and more decisions about food may be driven by an effort to prevent uncomfortable physical sensations.

Weight Loss

Some people initially restrict food because of physical symptoms without having significant concerns about weight or appearance. Illness and dietary restriction, however, can result in weight loss, and that can introduce another set of concerns.

Other people may comment positively on the weight loss, or the person may notice changes in their body that they like. What began as an effort to avoid physical discomfort can gradually become intertwined with a desire to maintain the lower weight. Returning to previously avoided foods may then raise concerns about both feeling physically unwell and gaining weight.

ARFID, Anorexia, and Other Presentations

For some people, fear of physical consequences remains at the center of the eating problem. Someone who has experienced significant pain, vomiting, choking, or other frightening symptoms may become intensely afraid of eating. In some cases, this may develop into avoidant restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID), in which restriction is not primarily driven by concerns about weight or shape.

article continues after advertisement

For others, restriction eventually becomes connected to weight, shape, or a desire to control eating and may look more like anorexia nervosa or another eating disorder. Understanding what is driving the restriction is important because treatment needs to address the factors that are keeping the eating problem going.

Treating Both

One of the complexities in these situations is that a legitimate medical problem and an eating disorder can exist at the same time, and both need to be taken seriously. Physical symptoms should not automatically be dismissed as anxiety simply because someone has an eating disorder. At the same time, having a genuine medical condition does not mean that every food rule or avoidance behavior remains medically necessary.

Treatment often requires collaboration among medical providers, eating disorder clinicians, and dietitians to clarify which dietary restrictions remain necessary while helping the patient challenge restrictions and fears that have moved beyond the original medical need.

For some people, a health condition becomes the catalyst for an eating disorder, as necessary attention to food and physical symptoms gradually becomes more restrictive, consuming, and driven by fear. Recognizing this progression early can make it possible to address the eating disorder while continuing to take the underlying medical condition and the person's physical experience seriously.

item.title: 4 Surprising Ways Your Anger Makes You Stronger
item.description:
Anger

4 Surprising Ways Your Anger Makes You Stronger

If you were taught to fear your anger, here's how to make it work for you.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Anger is one of the hardest feelings for emotionally neglected people to feel, name, or use.
  • Suppressed anger doesn't disappear; it returns stronger and loses all its usefulness.
  • Research links anger to motivation, better relationships, self-insight, and stronger negotiation.
Source: Krakenimages/AdobeStock

Of all human emotions, the one that people struggle with the most is anger. That's understandable.

After all, it's the emotion with the most potential to get us into trouble. It can be exquisitely uncomfortable, and it's the most difficult to control. As a psychologist, I have watched this one particular feeling cause more struggle than any other.

Some people find it easier to push their anger away, or suppress it, to avoid the discomfort and conflict it can bring. Others wear their anger like armor in hopes it will protect them from being hurt or mistreated. Still another group may go back and forth between pushing their anger down and erupting. In fact, these two things go together. The more you suppress your anger, the more intense it will be when it finally erupts.

If you were raised by parents who had low tolerance for your feelings (childhood emotional neglect), then you may be all too good at pushing your anger away so that you don't even have to feel it. In fact, you may, especially if you grew up this way, be so uncomfortable with the A-word that you find it almost impossible to say, “I’m angry.”

I'm frustrated, I'm annoyed, or I'm anxious, you may say, so you don’t have to say, “I'm angry.”If you're not comfortable with your anger, you're more likely to misread and mislabel it as something milder or more diffuse.

"Isn't stopping yourself from feeling angry a good skill to have?" you may be wondering. The answer is actually a resounding no. Research has shown how very important anger is to living a healthy life.

4 Reasons to Make Friends With Your Anger

1. Anger is a powerful motivator.

Aarts et al. (2010) found that people who were shown a picture of an angry face were more driven to obtain an object they were shown later. Anger is like a driver that pushes you to strive for what you want or need. It carries with it the message, "Act!"

Without anger: Alana was getting weary of being overlooked at work. She was well known to be skilled and reliable, and yet she was repeatedly passed over for promotion. Silently, she watched younger, less experienced employees move past her, one by one.

With anger: Alana became angry when a less-experienced colleague was promoted. "I deserve an explanation for this. I have to get myself promoted or leave the company," she realized. The next day she walked into her supervisor's office and asked why she was passed over. She was promised the next promotion slot.

2. Anger can make your relationship stronger.

Baumeister et al. (1990) found that hiding anger in intimate relationships can be detrimental. When you hide your anger from your partner, you're bypassing an important message that he or she may very much need to hear. Of course, it's important to take great care in how you express it. Try to calibrate it to the situation and express it with as much compassion for your partner as you can.

Without anger: Lance was tired of his wife Joanne's clutter. She kept, it seemed to Lance, virtually everything, and he wanted the spare room for an office. "I'll never get that room," he thought resignedly. All this time, Joanne had no idea there was a problem.

With anger: Lance was fed up. He told Joanne that the clutter was making him feel stressed, unhappy, and also angry at her. After several heated discussions, Joanne cleared her things from the spare room so Lance could make it his office. They made a truce to try to meet each other in the middle.

3. Anger can help you better understand yourself.

Kassinove et al. (1997) asked a large sample of people how recent outbursts of anger had affected them. Fifty-five percent said that getting angry had led to a positive outcome, and many said the episode had given them insight into their own faults. Anger can help you see yourself more clearly, and it can motivate self-change.

Without anger: "That's too bad, you'll just have to deal with it," Joanne said dully while exiting the room. She promptly put it out of her mind, because she didn't want to think about it.

With anger: "That's too bad, you'll just have to deal with it," Joanne fired back, then stormed out and slammed the door. Sitting on her bed, she felt enraged and criticized. But a few hours later, after thinking it through, she developed a different perspective. She looked around and saw her home as though through Lance's eyes. She could see why the clutter would be bothering him. "I need to get better at taking criticism," she thought.

4. Anger helps you negotiate.

In a study of negotiation by Van Kleef et al. (2004), people made larger concessions and fewer demands of participants who were angry than of ones who were not. Anger makes you more powerful, especially when it's justified and expressed with thought and care.

With anger: Alana knew she was angry, and that she needed to manage that anger if she wanted to be effective. She walked in and said, "I need to talk to you about something important." She explained how upset she was by her co-worker's promotion. Her boss said the co-worker was an excellent employee, which made Alana even angrier. "Yes, he's really good. But so am I, and I have more experience," she stated clearly. Her boss paused, surprised at Alana's persistence. "You're right," she said, and promised Alana the next available promotion.

Stop Saying STOP to Your Anger

If you grew up emotionally ignored, or in an environment that didn’t have the room or tolerance for you to get angry (childhood emotional neglect), some small part of your brain probably screams "STOP!" as soon as you get an inkling of anger. None of this was your fault, and very possibly it was not your parents' fault either. Most parents who cannot make room for anger were never taught to accept or understand their own.

The reality is that it's not easy to turn this around, but you can do it. Start thinking of your anger as a helpful emotion, not something to avoid. Pay attention to your anger, and try to notice when you're feeling it. Stop saying "STOP!" to your anger. Instead, listen to its message, consciously manage the feeling, and let your anger motivate and energize you.

Anger, when properly managed and expressed, is power. So when you suppress your anger, you're suppressing your power.

And why would you do that?

A version of this post also appears on emotionalneglect.com.

© Jonice Webb, Ph.D.

item.title: 5 Essential Skills of Self-Mastery
item.description:
Coaching

5 Essential Skills of Self-Mastery

How to coach yourself toward a more conscious and fulfilling life.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Personal responsibility gives you the power to become the author of your life.
  • Non-judgmental mindfulness creates space between what you feel and what you do.
  • Self-compassion turns inner struggle into an opportunity for understanding and growth.
Source: AI-Generated

We spend much of our lives trying to master the world around us. Yet one of the most important forms of mastery receives far less attention: the ability to understand and manage ourselves.

Self-mastery does not mean controlling our emotion, eliminating vulnerability, or becoming perfect. Self-mastery is the ability to develop a conscious relationship with ourselves: to understand what is happening inside us, recognize the forces influencing our behavior, and increasingly choose how we want to respond.

In this sense, we can learn to become our own coach. A good coach helps us become curious, recognize patterns, challenge assumptions, identify what matters, and translate awareness into action. We can learn to cultivate these same capacities within ourselves.

Five interconnected skills can help us move from automatic reactions toward greater self-mastery: personal responsibility, self-observation and reflection, non-judgmental mindfulness, compassion, and conscious response.

1. Personal Responsibility: Becoming the Author of Your Life

Personal responsibility is the foundation of self-mastery because meaningful change becomes difficult when we consistently locate the source of our experience outside ourselves.

It is easy to believe that we would feel better if our spouse were more loving, our boss more appreciative, our children more cooperative, our parents had treated us better, or life had simply been fairer. Certainly, other people affect us profoundly, and many circumstances are outside our control.

Personal responsibility does not mean denying these realities or blaming ourselves for everything that happens. Rather, responsibility asks a more empowering question: Given what has happened, what is mine to do now?

When we accept this responsibility, we move from being merely a character in the story of our life toward becoming more of its author.

2. Self-Observation and Reflection: Being the Scientist of Yourself

One of the most powerful skills we can cultivate is the ability to observe ourselves with curiosity. I often encourage people to become scientists of their own inner world. Instead of simply living through an experience, we can also learn to study it.

article continues after advertisement

What am I feeling? What am I thinking? What happens in my body when I become anxious or angry? What situations repeatedly trigger me? What do I tend to do when I feel rejected, criticized, ashamed, or afraid? What am I trying to protect? What do I really need?

Self-observation also requires examining our beliefs. We often treat beliefs as facts simply because we have repeated them for many years: I am not good enough. People cannot be trusted. I must succeed to have value. Conflict is dangerous. If someone rejects me, something must be wrong with me.

A useful self-coaching practice is to question these assumptions: What am I believing right now? How do I know it is true? Is there another interpretation? What might become possible if I stopped organizing my life around this belief?

Introspection and awareness become valuable when they help us recognize the patterns that have been quietly directing our lives.

3. Non-Judgmental Mindfulness: Seeing Clearly Without Immediately Condemning

We notice jealousy and say, I shouldn't feel this way. We become anxious and think, What is wrong with me? We make a mistake and conclude, I'm such an idiot. Instead of observing our experience, we begin fighting with ourselves about having the experience.

Non-judgmental mindfulness offers another way: learning to notice thoughts, feelings, impulses, and bodily sensations without immediately categorizing them as good or bad.

We can say, I notice that I am angry, rather than becoming consumed by anger. We can recognize, Part of me wants to attack, without attacking. We can observe, I am afraid of being rejected, without automatically allowing that fear to determine our behavior.

This small shift, from being the experience to observing the experience, can create an enormous amount of freedom.

4. Cultivating Compassion: Meeting Yourself With Humanity

Awareness alone is not sufficient. What also matters is the quality of the relationship we develop with what we discover.

If self-observation becomes another opportunity to criticize ourselves, greater awareness may simply produce greater shame. This is why compassion is essential to self-mastery.

article continues after advertisement

Compassion means understanding that our reactions usually have a history and a purpose. The person who becomes defensive may have learned early that criticism was dangerous. The person who desperately seeks reassurance may carry a deep fear of abandonment. The perfectionist may have learned that achievement was the safest route toward approval and worthiness.

When we approach these patterns compassionately, we become curious rather than condemning. We might ask: What is this part of me trying to protect? What is it afraid would happen if it stopped doing this? What does it need from me?

Paradoxically, accepting ourselves often makes change easier rather than harder. Shame says, there is something wrong with me. Compassion says, something inside me is struggling, and I want to understand it.

From that position, growth becomes less of a war against ourselves and more of a process of integration.

5. Conscious Response: Creating the Space to Choose

The previous four skills lead to the ability to consciously choose our response.

Much of human behavior is reactive. Someone criticizes us and we defend ourselves. We feel rejected and withdraw. We become angry and attack. We feel insecure and seek reassurance. These reactions can happen so quickly that they feel inevitable, but they are not.

Between what happens to us and what we do next, there is a space. In this space lies our freedom. Self-mastery is largely about expanding that space.

When we take responsibility, observe ourselves, suspend judgment, and bring compassion to our experience, we create enough room to ask a different question:

article continues after advertisement

Who do I want to be in this moment?

That question moves toward a conscious response. It invites us to ask: What response reflects my values? What would serve my relationship? What will I respect tomorrow? What would the wiser version of myself choose?

What might your wiser self ask of you today so you can become the person you want to be? What would that person encourage you to let go of, confront, practice, or choose?

Self-mastery is not achieved through one dramatic transformation. It develops through thousands of small moments in which we become a little more aware and a little less automatic.

From Automatic Living to Conscious Living

A fulfilling life is a life that increasingly reflects who we genuinely want to be. That requires the courage to take responsibility for our lives, the curiosity to observe ourselves honestly, the mindfulness to see without immediate judgment, the compassion to embrace our humanity, and the discipline to choose our responses consciously.

We will still become angry, afraid, insecure, disappointed, and confused. Self-mastery does not remove the complexity of being human. It changes our relationship with that complexity.

So, next time you face difficult situation, ask yourself, “What is happening inside me, what can I learn from it, and how do I want to respond?” That may be one of the most important questions you can ask when coaching yourself.
